approachQuestion.prompt: A timer must be filled with an ordered sequence of actions. Each action has a duration from a list of distinct positive integers; durations may be reused. Return the number of duration sequences totaling exactly T, modulo 1000000007. Different orders count separately. Examples: durations=[1,2], T=3 → 3 ([1,1,1],[1,2],[2,1]); durations=[2,4], T=5 → 0. Which approach is most suitable?
constraints: 1 ≤ k=durations.length ≤ 30; distinct durations from 1 through 1000; 1 ≤ T ≤ 10000. Inputs are read-only. Return only a modular count.

options.text: Initialize ways[0]=1. For each total s from 1 through T, start its count at zero and add ways[s−v] for every duration v≤s, modulo the modulus. Return ways[T].
options.feedback: Every nonempty sequence has a unique last duration and a shorter total. Summing over all possible final durations counts all orders without duplicating the same ordered sequence.

options.text: Use this same sum-first recurrence, but also retain a row of counts for each total broken down by final duration, obtaining each total by summing its row.
options.feedback: This computes the correct result on the whole domain, but retains old states that future transitions never read. Removing those states preserves correctness and reduces auxiliary storage.

options.text: Process durations outside and update sums upward inside, as for unordered combinations.
options.feedback: For durations=[1,2], T=3, this merges [1,2] and [2,1], returning 2 rather than 3.

options.text: For every reachable total record only true instead of its count, then return one for a reachable target.
options.feedback: For durations=[1,2], T=3, three sequences exist but a Boolean state reports only one.

feedback.reason: Count ordered constructions by their unique final action, contrasting with type-first combination counting.
details: Allocate T+1 counters. For every total s=1..T, check every one of k durations and add the shorter-total count when legal. Do not exit early. Return ways[T].

Choose the last action at every total. Because total is the outer loop, different action orders contribute separately. Reversing the loops would count multisets rather than the ordered sequences requested here.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Allocate T+1 counters. For every total s=1..T, check every one of k durations and add the shorter-total count when legal. Do not exit early. Return ways[T]. Analyze this fixed implementation. N=k; k,T vary independently. Choose the tightest worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair.
constraints: Array indexing and word arithmetic take constant time. No hashing, amortized containers, recursion, slicing, or input copying is used. Count all allocated work arrays and temporaries; exclude the read-only input and scalar output.
Include initialization; treat the stated dimensions as variable parameters within their bounds. Use a word per stored counter or flag, not a packed bitset.

feedback.reason: Every positive total checks all k durations in one count array.
details: Every one of T totals checks k durations. Initialization takes T+1 work, dominated because k,T are positive. One total-count array is live, with no sequence lists or call stack.
“O(T) time, O(T) auxiliary space”: Every total checks k durations, and k is a variable parameter.
“O(kT) time, O(kT) auxiliary space”: The array stores totals only; no per-final-duration table is retained.
“O(kT) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: Counting each total still requires T+1 counters for shorter totals.
